title: Political notes: Pelosi honored, Women’s Hall grows, but it’s still tough for women
summary: Three women speakers share the limelight in the House, three women legislators are recognized with the First Citizen Award, more women are inducted into the Maryland Women's Hall of Fame -- but it's still tough to be a woman legislator, in political notes.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters March 31, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters March 31, 2026

Baltimore-born Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) was given a warm “welcome home” by the General Assembly and Gov. Wes Moore (D) Monday, in a day chock-full of events honoring her legacy as the first female speaker of the U.S. House, as she winds down the last term of her lengthy political career.

Pelosi’s day in Annapolis started in Government House, where Moore hosted a breakfast in honor of Pelosi, who he said will always be “a daughter of Baltimore.”

The event was closed to press, but in a social media post about it, Moore was quoted as saying Pelosi “is an absolute force of nature. While I know your heart and your representation might belong to San Francisco, she is Maryland Tough and Baltimore Strong.”

Her day in Annapolis continued Monday evening, when Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) honored Pelosi with the First Citizen Award, presented to “Marylanders who have been dedicated and effective participants in making government work for the benefit of all,” according to the Maryland State House website.

After missing most of the session, Benson, Jones return to praise, affection, flowers

Pelosi was awarded for her leadership while in Congress, a legacy she solidified with her “direct manner, steely nerve and willingness to confront her adversaries,” according to remarks by State Archivist Elaine Rice Bachmann.

She was one of three First Citizen recipients Monday, along with Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince Georges) and former Maryland House Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County).

Pelosi said she was honored to receive the recognition and will “display it with great pride for the time I have left in the Capitol.”

“It means so much to me personally, politically, officially – in every way,” Pelosi said.

At one point Monday, the Maryland House had three women in the chamber who have held the title House speaker.

Before calling Pelosi to speak to the chamber, House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) noted that her predecessor, former Speaker Jones, was sitting in the gallery. Delegates jumped their feet for a standing ovation for the former speaker, who has not been seen at her desk since the start of session.

“Speaker Adrienne Jones, you must feel the love right now, because we love you and miss you,” Peña-Melnyk said.

Peña-Melnyk presented Pelosi with a resolution, noting that Pelosi’s career “has proven over and over that a woman can lead with great skill, tremendous conviction and fearless determination.”

“Once a Marylander, always a Marylander,” Peña-Melnyk said. “And so, Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to say to you: Welcome home.”

Pelosi noted that her father, Thomas Ludwig John D’Alesandro Jr., was elected to the Maryland House of Delegates in 1926 to represent Baltimore’s 1st District – a century ago.

“Our family is just so thrilled to be with all of you here,” she told the House chamber. “As a first woman Speaker of the House of Representatives, imagine how exciting it is for me to be in a body of legislators that has had two women speakers.”

Not every legislator was stoked to see Pelosi being honored in the State House. Several left the room during her recognition in that chamber Monday evening, though some stayed for her remarks.

And across the hall, Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) questioned whether Pelosi embodied the First Citizen Award she received in the Senate.

“Speaker Nancy Pelosi has had a long and consequential career as a representative from California, but she is also widely recognized as one of the most polarizing political figures of our time,”  Hershey said in a written statement. “I don’t believe elevating that record reflects the kind of leadership Marylanders would choose to recognize as ‘First Citizen.’”

It wasn’t just Pelosi honored Monday in the waning days of Women’s History Month: Her mother, Annunciata “Nancy” Lombardi D’Alesandro (1909-1995) was inducted into the Maryland Women’s Hall of Fame Monday evening, along with seven other influential Maryland women.

Each year, the Maryland Commission for Women selects a handful of notable figures, both living and passed, to induct into the Hall, honoring trailblazers in politics, science, military service and other fields.

D’Alesandro was inducted for her advocacy for housing, employment and other social services, particularly for immigrant communities, during her time as the first lady to 41st Baltimore Mayor Thomas Ludwig John D’Alesandro Jr. She was also the mother of Baltimore’s 44th Mayor Thomas D’Alesandro III.

Perez was commissioned as an officer in the U.S. Army Medical Service Corps in 2005, and died a year later while deployed in Iraq, after an improvised explosive device struck her vehicle.

Former Maryland Sen. Delores Kelley was inducted for more than 30 years of service in the General Assembly, first in the House from 1991 to 1995 and then in the Senate for almost 30 years, until 2023. The Baltimore County Democrat was the first woman to chair the Finance Committee, where she promoted health care access and long-term care.

Their inclusion will add to the more than 100 names in the Woman’s Hall of Fame.

Improving access to child care. Helping formerly incarcerated women return to society. Coverage for perinatal mental health screening. Those are just a handful of legislative issues women in the Maryland Senate have been focusing on this session, highlighted during a news conference Monday afternoon.

Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) invited members of the Senate Women’s Caucus to talk about their legislative priorities this session that directly or indirectly impact Maryland’s women.

But a challenging truth still hung overhead – women make up just under 30% of the Senate, leading some of the speakers to admit that they lean on their male colleagues for support to push issues through.

For many of the senators speaking Monday, it’s still important to look at the progress women have made – even if there is still more to do for women in the Senate and women in Maryland.

“Women’s leadership in the Maryland Senate didn’t happen overnight. It was built through decades of persistence and advocacy and breaking barriers,” Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County) said Monday. “Today we stand in a Senate where women are shaping budgets, leading committees and driving policy that impacts families across Maryland.”

Sen. Pam Beidle (D-Anne Arundel) and Sen. Nancy J. King (D-Montgomery) reflected that it can be hard to get young women to run for office, especially if young children are involved. But they hope that they and other women in leadership can mentor up-and-coming legislators

“I think it’s really difficult for women to step up, and that’s what all of us need to do, is to help other women and young women run for office,” Beidle said. “I think we really do bring a different perspective.”

King added that the long hours of the 90-day legislative session can add on to those challenges.

“You really kind of take your life and you set it aside for three months, and especially for somebody with young children, it’s really hard to do that,” King said. “We’re here all day and late into the night. If you don’t have a spouse that can really do the other half of that, you’re really stuck. I think that’s what chases women away. I’m hoping we have more women getting elected this year.”
